blocks.text: Light displays a dual nature: it acts as a wave and as a particle. Assuming symmetry in nature, the French physicist Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that particles should also have wave-like properties. The momentum of a photon is p = h/lambda (18.3); de Broglie suggested that the momentum of a material particle of mass m moving with velocity v is given by the same expression: p = h/lambda = mv, or lambda = h/p = h/(mv) (18.10), where lambda is the wavelength of the particle wave. This is the de Broglie relation: an electron can be considered both a particle and a wave.

An object of large mass and ordinary speed has such a small wavelength that its wave effects, such as interference and diffraction, are negligible. A rifle bullet of mass 20 g flying at 330 m s^-1 has lambda = h/(mv) = 6.63 x 10^-34 / (2 x 10^-2 x 330) = 1 x 10^-34 m, far too small to measure. But an electron moving at 1 x 10^6 m s^-1 has lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / (9.1 x 10^-31 x 1 x 10^6) = 7 x 10^-10 m, in the X-ray range. So diffraction effects for electrons are measurable, whereas interference effects for bullets are not.

Convincing evidence for the wave nature of electrons was provided by Clinton J. Davisson and Lester H. Germer, who showed that electrons are diffracted by metal crystals in exactly the same way as X-rays. In their apparatus (Fig 18.7), electrons from a heated filament are accelerated by an adjustable voltage, and the beam is directed at a nickel crystal. The scattered electrons came off in regular peaks, which they interpreted as diffraction, just like X-ray diffraction by a crystal. The wavelength of the electron waves was just that predicted by de Broglie.

blocks.alt: An electron gun with a heated filament points its beam down at a nickel crystal. A dashed line from the crystal goes to a detector that slides along a curved scale; the angle between the incident and the scattered beam is phi.
blocks.caption: Figure 18.7: Experimental arrangement of Davisson and Germer for electron diffraction (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 18.7).

blocks.text: The gain in K.E. of an electron accelerated through a potential V is (1/2) mv^2 = Ve, so mv^2 = 2Ve, m^2 v^2 = 2mVe and mv = square root of (2mVe). From de Broglie's equation, lambda = h/(mv), so lambda = h / square root of (2mVe) (18.11). In one experiment V was 54 volts: lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / square root of (2 x 9.1 x 10^-31 x 54 x 1.6 x 10^-19) = 1.66 x 10^-10 m. The diffracted beam was found at a glancing angle of 65 degrees, and Bragg's equation 2d sin(theta) = m lambda, with m = 1 and d = 0.91 x 10^-10 m for nickel, gives lambda = 2 x 0.91 x 10^-10 x sin 65 degrees = 1.65 x 10^-10 m: excellent agreement with the prediction.

Diffraction patterns have also been observed with protons, neutrons, hydrogen atoms and helium atoms, giving substantial evidence for the wave nature of particles. De Broglie received the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physics; Clinton Davisson and George Paget Thomson shared the 1937 Nobel Prize for confirming the wave nature of particles by experiment.
